##### **Status quo of work time reduction in 40 organizations as of February 2026** organizations as of February 2026
Overall, 22% have adapted their model since the end of the trial period. The most frequently cited reason for these changes is that the original 4DW format was perceived as too rigid for everyday operations. One organization summarized this by stating that _"the model worked well in principle, but it was too inflexible for our day-to-day operations.“_ As a result, many of these organizations have moved towards more flexible arrangements that allow greater variation depending on teams, roles, and business needs. These adaptations include models with defined weekly reductions, monthly working time targets, or rotation systems. 6 Working Time Models WORK TIME REDUCTION IN GERMANY It is also important to note that reduced working time has not been introduced across entire organizations in every case. In several organizations, the model is still being piloted or has only been implemented in specific parts of the organization. Additionally, the path has not always been linear. One organization, for example, suspended the WTR between March and December 2025 due to a short-term order peak, but reintroduced the model in January 2026 once the situation had stabilized. Other organizations reported that current economic pressure and, in some cases, layoffs influenced both the pace and scope of the rollout. Among the 30% of organizations that no longer operate a reduced working week, economic and operational factors play a central role. Workload peaks, volatile business conditions, or structural constraints made it difficult to sustain reduced hours in a reliable way. One organization explained that _"we simply could not guarantee reliable delivery with reduced hours during high-demand phases,"_ while another reported that _"the uncertainty in our market forced us to prioritize shortterm capacity over long-term experiments."_

Two years after the start of the trial, the landscape is characterized by diversity rather than uniformity. While a clear majority of organizations have maintained a WTR, the specific models in use have diversified further. At the same time, the share of organizations who have returned to conventional schedules, underscore that WTR is not a straightforward undertaking. The extent to which organizations were able to sustain the model appears closely linked to their economic conditions, operational demands, and willingness to adapt the original format. These findings suggest that the longterm viability of WTR depends not only on initial enthusiasm, but also on an organization's capacity to absorb and respond to the practical challenges that emerge over time.

In parallel, the legal right to part-time work and possible restrictions are also under discussion, prompted in part by initiatives from business-oriented circles within the Union parties, which seek to tie part-time work more closely to specific justifications (Süddeutsche Zeitung, 2026. This has sparked further political debate about the scope of employee rights (Deutscher Bundestag, 2026. 

Against this backdrop, the German pilot study on the 4DW revealed a nuanced impact profile at both the organizational and employee levels. In terms of performance and productivity, key financial indicators remained broadly stable despite reduced working hours and less overtime. Employer attractiveness appeared to benefit from higher life satisfaction and improved retention. 

Regarding health, employees reported improvements, supported by increased physical activity and longer sleep duration, though no clear reduction in absenteeism was observed. Leisure activities also gained more space, with participants reporting more time for family, recreation, and self-care (Backmann et al., 2024. Early international research on WTR similarly points to positive effects on employee well-being (Fan et al., 2025. 

At the same time, the German trial also surfaced initial indications that the transition to reduced working hours is not a guaranteed success. It can entail costs, organizational challenges, and a risk of failure. Moreover, evidence on the long-term sustainability of work time reduction (WTR initiatives and their positive effects remains limited, a particularly pressing gap given that the social, political, and economic conditions outlined above place additional pressure on such initiatives.

Study Context 



###### **The aim of this update report is therefore to track further developments in the participating organizations and assess their status roughly two years after the start of the trial.** 

The focus is on the stability of the models introduced, possible adjustments, alternative forms of working time arrangements, as well as the reasons for and outcomes of transitions back to full-time schedules. 

To this end, we first provide an update on key findings regarding the continued or adapted implementation of the 4DW, before highlighting the developments observable over time.

# **2. Development of Working Time Models Until 2026** In October 2024, 73% of the 41 participating organizations stated after the trial period that they would continue the 4DW beyond the test period, either by extending it or implementing it on a permanent basis. In contrast, 20% decided against continuing, and 7% remained undecided. ##### **Implementation of the four-day-week in 41 organizations after completion of the trial period as of October 2024** organizations after completion of the trial period
as of October 2024
Please note, this report no longer speaks primarily of a "four-day-week," but of "work time reduction". Already during the trial period, it became apparent that the label "four-day-week" did not fully capture the variety of models introduced. While the original trial was widely associated with a fixed day off per week, some organizations started to adopt more flexible arrangements even within the trial period. This trend has continued and become more pronounced since. Many organizations have moved towards flexible weekly reductions, monthly hour targets, or rotationbased systems that no longer correspond to a classic four-day format. What these diverse models share is not a particular schedule structure, but a reduction in total working hours. WTR is therefore the more accurate and analytically appropriate umbrella term as it captures the common denominator across all models without implying a specific format. Of the 41 organizations that completed the pilot, 40 participated in our follow-up survey, on which this report is based. As of February 2026, 70% of these organizations operate with some form of WTR, while 30% do not. The overall picture since the last report is one of consolidation. Most organizations that were previously in an extended trial phase have now either transitioned into full implementation — in some cases in an adapted form — or have discontinued the model altogether. Only in a small number of cases was an initial decision to continue later reversed. At the same time, the 30% that no longer practice WTR underscore that that sustaining such models is not straightforward for all organizations.

# **Statement from the Initiators** 

Over the past twelve months, the impression emerged that the debate around the four-day workweek in Germany had lost momentum with the federal elections. Discussions about work time reduction gave way to calls for longer hours and a more critical stance toward part-time arrangements. The question emerged: Had the chapter of “New Work” — to which the four-day week undoubtedly belongs — come to an end? 

From our perspective as practice partners of the study, however, what we observed was not an ending but rather a shift: **from public hype to a more focused and serious examination.** Organizations today are less concerned with symbolic models and more focused on the fundamental question of how productivity, efficiency, and employer attractiveness can be designed in a way that remains viable under real economic conditions. 

This is precisely where the findings of the update report resonate with our experience in organizational development: **Companies are no longer searching for an ideological 4-or-5-day solution, but for a sustainable mix of structure, flexibility, and performance orientation.** Working time is increasingly understood as a design variable rather than a dogma — especially in a moment in time where AI-based tools are beginning to redefine how work itself is organized and executed. What matters most is the ability to adapt models, sharpen processes, and actively involve employees in this transformation. 

**Working time reduction is not a golden bullet; it is a change process.** And like any meaningful change process, it requires investment, leadership, and clarity. The report underlines that the real challenge lies less in the specific model and more in the adaptability of people and organizations. The broader questions it raises — about the relationship of work, life, and performance — have also guided our thinking beyond the study in our capacity as Consultants. 



**Thus, the report offers an alternative perspective on the current economic policy debate in Germany.** It suggests that performance does not necessarily result from increasing working hours, but rather from smarter work organization, clearer prioritization, and adaptive structures. With or without a four-day week, the decisive factor is not the number of working days, but an organization’s ability to design work in a way that allows performance, health, and innovation to reinforce one another over the long term.

#### **Carsten Meier** 

_Initiator 4 Tage Woche Deutschland Co-Author WORK LIFE REMIX Co-Founder Intraprenör_ 

The long-term results of the report point to one central insight: **Piloting new ways of working pays off.** It pays off when models are permanently implemented — reflected in stronger employer attractiveness, stable performance, and improved well-being. It also pays off when organizations ultimately decide not to continue. Even in those cases, valuable insights emerge regarding efficiency, prioritization, and organizational limits.

# **5. Conclusion** 

The results of this update report show that a majority of organizations continue to operate with some form of WTR more than a year after the end of the pilot phase. At the same time, the classic 4DW has become less central. Many organizations have moved towards broader and more flexible forms of WTR that better accommodate their operational realities. This shift was already observable during the trial period and the continued adaptation of WTR models since then reinforces a key finding: the practical viability of WTR appears to depend less on adherence to a fixed format and more on an organization's willingness and capacity to adapt the model over time. 

However, the findings also make clear that these models do not come without costs. Regardless of whether organizations continued or discontinued reduced working time, the implementation process required sustained management attention, coordination effort, and, in some cases, came with productivity losses or delays during the implementation phase. WTR should therefore not be understood as a simple efficiency gain, but as a structural change process that involves trade-offs, transitional friction, and real implementation costs independent of the final outcome. 

At the individual level, the employee data paints a differentiated picture. Employees currently working under reduced hours consistently report more favorable outcomes across stress, burnout, mental health, and several performance dimensions. Yet these advantages are not equally pronounced across all domains. Life satisfaction and creativity at work do not significantly differ. Meanwhile, employees who returned to a conventional schedule occupy a distinct middle position. The finding that this group reports the lowest physical health scores while also reporting the highest financial satisfaction may point to inherent trade-offs that WTR involves at the individual level. 

Importantly, these findings are cross-sectional and self-reported, and the possibility of selection effects, whereby employees and organizations that continued with WTR differ systematically from those that did not, should be kept in mind. 

At the same time, many organizations report substantial benefits, ranging from improved employer attractiveness and employee satisfaction to more sustainable ways of working. Even among those that no longer use WTR, these benefits are often acknowledged, though they may be outweighed by operational or economic constraints in the specific organizational context. Conversely, the 30% of organizations that discontinued the model serve as an important reminder that WTR is not universally viable. Workload peaks, volatile market conditions, and structural constraints can render it unsustainable regardless of employee preferences.

##### **Impact on Work-Life Balance** 



These findings suggest clear, almost universally positive effects on employee work-life balance, which is in line with findings from early academic research (Fan et al., 2025, and might explain the positive effects on employer attractiveness and employee retention. 

These findings further support the existing evidence from academic literature, echoing positive effects on turnover and satisfaction but less conclusive implications for employee health (Campbell, 2024, whereas we find little evidence for the long-standing assertion that these positive effects may fade over time, which might be more relevant to the case of work time compression (see e.g., Nord & Costigan, 1973; Ivancevic & Lyon, 1977 rather than our case of WTR. 

It is important to note, however, that our findings reflect self-reported perceptions from a subset of organizations that have chosen to continue with WTR. Organizations that discontinued the model, discussed in the following section, may have had different experiences, which introduces a potential selection effect. As such, the results should be interpreted descriptively and do not permit causal conclusions about the effects of WTR. 

##### **Impact on Work Conditions** 



Taken together, these descriptive distributions indicate that, among organizations still implementing WTR, the perceived direction of change is predominantly favorable across most dimensions particularly for innovation and creativity, employer attractiveness and retention, and working conditions and work-life balance. Applicant quality and sick leave, by contrast, show a larger share of unchanged responses, suggesting that these domains may be slower to shift or less directly affected by the reduction in working time.

But Germany was far from being the only country to benefit from the use of short-time work/worksharing during this crisis. In their comparative analysis, Hijzen and Venn (2011) found that among the 34 countries in the OECD, 24 countries used short-time work or comparable instruments during the global financial crisis; in 22 of them, either these regulations were newly introduced or existing regulations were expanded and adapted to the challenges of the crisis. An important distinguishing criterion of these schemes was the extent of the permitted reduction of hours of work: 15 countries set a lower limit for the reduction, ranging from 10 to 40 per cent of contractual weekly hours of work, while in the other countries weekly hours of work could also be reduced to zero. Most countries also presupposed agreements by the social partners in the companies and/or a justification of the economic necessity for this scheme, so that the share of state subsidies and the labour costs remaining with the companies differed significantly among countries, as did the employees’ entitlement to earned income. This was also true for the maximum duration of benefits, which ranged from three months to two years or more; countries with short durations of short-time work were mostly more generous in the amount of shorttime compensation benefits. 

More important in the context of working-time effects, however, was the actual use of work-sharing/ short-time work. Hijzen and Venn found that the highest shares of employees on short-time work in 2009 were observed in Belgium (just under 6 per cent), Türkiye (4 per cent) and Italy, Germany and Japan (about 3 per cent each). The manufacturing sector was the main focus of short-time work; in a comparison of these and other countries, about 9 per cent of employees were on short-time work in this sector in 2009. This was followed at a considerable distance by the construction sector, where the share was just under 3 per cent. However, countries differed greatly in terms of the reductions in hours of work associated with short-time work. Whereas in Spain, Finland and Norway this was about 90 per cent or more of full-time hours of work, the reduction in countries listed with high usage during the global financial crisis was significantly lower, at about 40 per cent in Belgium, approximately 30 per cent in Türkiye and just under 30 per cent in Japan and Germany.

Overall, the health-related findings present a differentiated picture. Employees who continue to work reduced hours consistently report the most favorable outcomes across stress, mental health, burnout, and physical health. The Control group, which never experienced a change in working time, tends to report the least favorable values — particularly for mental health and burnout.

**Ultimately, the results suggest that there is no single "right" model.** For some organizations, the advantages clearly outweigh the costs, while for others the balance tilts in the opposite direction. The key insight is that success depends less on adopting a specific format and more on finding a version of WTR that fits the organization's strategy, structure, and business reality and on being prepared to adapt that version as circumstances change.

The introduction and development of this type of short-term working-time flexibility instruments has long been the focus of companies and employees alike. In industrial production areas, in addition to the classic form of overtime work, working-time accounts, which enabled companies to react quickly and easily to fluctuations in the order situation, became increasingly widespread. In the service sector, various forms of flextime work with so-called core working hours became established. Since the turn of the millennium, however, and increasingly in the last decade, there has been a growing interest in longterm or life-phase-related working-time flexibility, that is, measures that take into account the different time requirements and availabilities of employees over the life course. These measures may be occasionrelated (parental or care leaves, qualification phases) but may also take into account new life concepts and allow temporary time off or working-time reductions without explicit reasons (long-term workingtime accounts; sabbaticals; the new Brückenteilzeit in Germany, which grants temporary part-time work with a right to return to the previous hours of work; and more recent collective bargaining agreements that allow employees to choose between a collectively agreed pay increase and time off). The more measures a company has already established, the more options it has to react spontaneously in times of crisis and the smoother the transition is likely to be. In this context, studies on home-office working during the pandemic, for example, show that the transition is faster and smoother when employees (or establishments) have had experience before the crisis (Frodermann et al. 2020). 

In sum, companies have at least potentially a wide range of instruments at their disposal that enables them to respond to changes in work volume demands by adjusting personnel and/ or hours of work. As the following analyses will show, almost all of these flexibility instruments were used in the current crisis in one country or another, sometimes in a modified form and sometimes in combination. 

However, this scope is sharpened and limited by both the political framework of working-time policy and institutional regulations. This is particularly true with regard to the question of limiting personnel fluctuations through regulations on protection against dismissal, collective agreements or company negotiations with interest groups. In countries such as the United Kingdom or the United States, in which these are weakly developed, the possibility is opened up for companies to rely on “hire and fire” strategies, while in countries with strong regulations, such as Germany and Sweden, working-time flexibility is likely to play a far greater role. 

112

##### **5.3.2 The financial crisis as a model** 

The current boom in state-funded reductions in hours of work discussed later in this chapter can be explained above all by the exemplary role it played as an instrument of labour market policy in overcoming the global financial market crisis about one decade ago. Here, it was countries such as Germany which, with the help of short-time work, were able to maintain significant proportions of their employment volume, especially in the industrial sectors that were threatened by drastic and abrupt falls in demand on the international goods markets; in some cases, these falls amounted to up to 40 per cent of pre-crisis levels. Not least because of this instrument (but also because of other forms of working-time reduction, such as the withdrawal of time from working-time accounts, the reduction of overtime and company agreements to reduce the number of weekly hours of work), hours of work were cut by approximately 40 hours per employee in 2009. Short-time work contributed to this by more than 13 hours (Fuchs et al. 2010). Although Germany’s gross domestic product fell by about 5 per cent that year, the volume of employment remained virtually constant. Admittedly, this was also due to a slight shift in employment to the service sector, which was not affected by the crisis due to stable domestic demand. However, the reduction in hours of work arithmetically prevented a decline in employment of approximately 3 per cent (Herzog-Stein and Seifert 2010). This development was very different from many other countries, where employment fell sharply with the economic slump. For this reason, there has been talk of a German “job miracle” in international comparisons (Bosch 2011).

##### **4.3.1 Life and job satisfaction** 

Working-time mismatches negatively affect the life satisfaction of overemployed workers, while results are more mixed for underemployed workers. The effect of hours of work on job satisfaction, as evidenced by self-determined hours of work for full-time employees, was found to be significantly positive (Hanglberger 2010, based on German Socio-Economic Panel (GSOEP) data for 2005 and 2007). Having a degree of control over their hours of work facilitates better working-time matches for workers, leading to a greater likelihood of job satisfaction. In an analysis focusing on overall life satisfaction (including job, family life and free time satisfaction), the desire to reduce their hours of work negatively impacted the job satisfaction of German workers (Holly and Mohenen 2012, based on GSOEP data for 2009). Nearly 60 per cent of German workers in 2009 desired to reduce their hours of work, representing a considerable proportion of the workforce. By contrast, multiple studies employing subjective measures of job satisfaction have been unable to detect sizeable negative associations with part-time work (Bardasi and Francesconi 2004; Blanchflower and Oswald 1998; Booth and van Ours 2007; D’Addio, Eriksson and Frijters 2007; Manning and Petrongolo 2004; Wooden and Warren 2004). In one of the few studies focusing on overemployment, Australian workers were found to have meaningful reductions in life satisfaction due to working more hours than they desired (Wooden, Warren and Drago 2009). This effect was significant for both sexes, although it was larger for men. Unsurprisingly, a study on the impact of underemployment on worker well-being using longitudinal data found little evidence to support the claim that underemployed workers have lower satisfaction than otherwise comparable fully employed workers (Friedland and Price 2003). Therefore, working-time mismatches negatively impact overemployed workers’ life satisfaction and job satisfaction, but there is more mixed evidence of such an impact for the underemployed.

### **3.2.  Organizations Without Work Time Reduction** 

The transition from a reduced working time model back to a standard schedule was associated with several perceived negative effects across the participating organizations. According to their reports, nearly all organizations identified a worsening of both working conditions and work-life balance as a consequence of returning to the original schedule, with all organizations specifically noting a deterioration in work-life balance. In terms of health-related indicators, some organizations reported that sick leave had worsened compared to the period during the reduced schedule. Regarding external positioning, a few organizations reported a decline in employer attractiveness. For all other areas surveyed, no changes were reported. 

Despite these predominantly unfavorable perceptions, most organizations did not encounter major difficulties during the transition itself. Although employees in most organizations did not support the decision to return to a standard schedule, this did not lead to significant operational disruptions such as resignations. In particular, when the reasons for discontinuing the WTR were clearly communicated, management reported that employees were generally understanding, even if not in agreement with the decision. 

Regarding future plans, the organizations without WTR are evenly split into three groups: one third remains undecided, one third has no concrete plans for future changes, and one third has concrete plans to reintroduce some form of work time adjustment. Notably, however, the organizations with concrete plans intend to prioritize work time compression (i.e., redistributing the same number of hours into fewer days) over an actual reduction in total working hours.

###### **Results** 

###### _(1) Real working-time reduction_ 

Opponents of the workweek reductions argued that that it would lead to increased overtime as employees would have to catch up outside normal working hours (Haraldsson and Kellam 2021). However, there was no evidence supporting this hypothesis in either pilot. Service provision remained at the same level, with the time reduction coming from “rethinking how tasks were completed: shortening meetings, cutting out unnecessary tasks, and shift arrangements” (Haraldsson and Kellam 2021). As a result, the workweek reduction was achieved through changes to working practises to ensure achieve efficiency of time use. 

###### _(2) Productivity increase and service provision_ 

The majority of data collected on the Icelandic trials suggests that service provision remained the same. The report (Haraldsson and Kellam 2021) contains detailed quantitative analysis of each department’s services and found a continuity of service quality as well. It can be extrapolated from these results that there was an increase in productivity given that the same service was provided with fewer hours of work.

#### **3.7. Conclusion** 

A variety of working-time arrangements currently exist in the global economy. This chapter has documented the prevalence of the most notable arrangements and their known effects on work–life balance, based on the limited data available. Better work–life balance, an important outcome of many of these arrangements, provides significant benefits for both employers and employees. It is therefore important to identify the work–life balance outcomes associated with each working-time arrangement. 

- X The classic standard workweek (8 hours per day, five or six days per week) provides stability to workers in planning their lives, yet such fixed schedules are often too inflexible to allow time for family demands as and when needed. 

- X Shift work may provide greater schedule flexibility to workers to help them balance work and nonwork commitments. However, shift work may require workers to work during atypical hours, which has been linked to significant health risks and family life disruptions. 

- X Part-time work (less than 35 hours per week) with predictable work schedules enables workers to have more time for their personal responsibilities and/or leisure, leading to a better balance between paid work and personal life. 

- X On-call work, based on highly unpredictable «just-in-time» schedules, severely disrupts work–life balance by making it difficult for workers to organize their personal lives and finances; it has also been shown to have negative effects on workers’ health. 

- X Flextime (flexible schedules) enables workers to organize their own work schedules based on their individual needs, within established parameters, in order to optimally balance their paid work and personal commitments. It has positive effects on workers’ mental health but may reinforce gender inequalities if only women use it. The dramatic increase in flexible working arrangements during the pandemic (especially telework) by both men and women suggests that this may be a less significant concern in the post-pandemic world (although research is needed to confirm this hypothesis). 

- X Compressed work weeks provide employees with longer weekends to spend with family and friends and thereby improve work–life balance; there is a debate about their health impacts, but the evidence trends towards positive effects. 

- X Finally, hours-averaging schemes with short-to-medium-term reference periods (such as one to four months) may facilitate work–life balance; however, if they are poorly designed and implemented, employees may be left vulnerable to drastic swings in hours of work that disrupt their personal lives.

In the service sector, various forms of flextime work with so-called core working hours became established. Since the turn of the millennium, however, and increasingly in the last decade, there has been a growing interest in longterm or life-phase-related working-time flexibility, that is, measures that take into account the different time requirements and availabilities of employees over the life course. In an analysis focusing on overall life satisfaction (including job, family life and free time satisfaction), the desire to reduce their hours of work negatively impacted the job satisfaction of German workers (Holly and Mohenen 2012, based on GSOEP data for 2009). Nearly 60 per cent of German workers in 2009 desired to reduce their hours of work, representing a considerable proportion of the workforce. Conclusion** A variety of working-time arrangements currently exist in the global economy. This chapter has documented the prevalence of the most notable arrangements and their known effects on work–life balance, based on the limited data available. Better work–life balance, an important outcome of many of these arrangements, provides significant benefits for both employers and employees. It is therefore important to identify the work–life balance outcomes associated with each working-time arrangement. - X The classic standard workweek (8 hours per day, five or six days per week) provides stability to workers in planning their lives, yet such fixed schedules are often too inflexible to allow time for family demands as and when needed. - X Shift work may provide greater schedule flexibility to workers to help them balance work and nonwork commitments. However, shift work may require workers to work during atypical hours, which has been linked to significant health risks and family life disruptions. - X Part-time work (less than 35 hours per week) with predictable work schedules enables workers to have more time for their personal responsibilities and/or leisure, leading to a better balance between paid work and personal life. - X On-call work, based on highly unpredictable «just-in-time» schedules, severely disrupts work–life balance by making it difficult for workers to organize their personal lives and finances; it has also been shown to have negative effects on workers’ health. - X Flextime (flexible schedules) enables workers to organize their own work schedules based on their individual needs, within established parameters, in order to optimally balance their paid work and personal commitments. It has positive effects on workers’ mental health but may reinforce gender inequalities if only women use it. The dramatic increase in flexible working arrangements during the pandemic (especially telework) by both men and women suggests that this may be a less significant concern in the post-pandemic world (although research is needed to confirm this hypothesis). - X Compressed work weeks provide employees with longer weekends to spend with family and friends and thereby improve work–life balance; there is a debate about their health impacts, but the evidence trends towards positive effects. - X Finally, hours-averaging schemes with short-to-medium-term reference periods (such as one to four months) may facilitate work–life balance; however, if they are poorly designed and implemented, employees may be left vulnerable to drastic swings in hours of work that disrupt their personal lives. 68 Working time and work-life balance around the world
